question: How can flexible regression, density estimation and classification be done by fitting simple models locally with kernel weights, and how do these tie to basis-function, mixture and structured models?
contributions: Nadaraya-Watson and local linear/polynomial regression, bias-variance in width and degree
Local regression in R^p, structured kernels, additive and varying-coefficient models
Local likelihood, kernel density estimation and classification, naive Bayes
Radial basis functions and Gaussian mixtures as kernel methods

results.claim: Local linear regression removes Nadaraya-Watson boundary bias exactly to first order (automatic kernel carpentry); local polynomial of degree d leaves only bias terms of degree d+1 and up
results.setup: 1-D local regression, any kernel, model yi=f(xi)+eps; Sec 6.1.1, eq 6.10
results.quote:
Local linear re-
gression automatically modiﬁes the kernel to correct the bias exactly to
ﬁrst order, a phenomenon dubbed as automatic kernel carpentry.

results.claim: Variance of a local regression fit is sigma^2 ||l(x0)||^2 and ||l|| grows with polynomial degree d, giving a bias-variance tradeoff in d
results.setup: Local polynomial regression, iid errors mean zero variance sigma^2; Sec 6.1.1
results.quote:
Var( ˆf(x0)) = σ2||l(x0)||2, where l(x0) is the vector of equivalent kernel
weights at x0.

results.claim: Local linear helps boundary bias dramatically at modest variance cost; local quadratic does little at the boundary but raises variance a lot and is most useful for interior curvature; odd degrees dominate even asymptotically
results.quote:
Local linear ﬁts can help bias dramatically at the boundaries at a
modest cost in variance.

results.claim: A local linear smoother with span 40% (tri-cube) has effective df = trace(S_lambda) = 5.86; a smoothing spline calibrated to the same df has a qualitatively similar equivalent kernel
results.setup: Fig 6.7 example, tri-cube kernel, span 40%; Sec 6.2
results.quote: The local regression smoother has a span of 40%, which results in df = trace(Sλ) = 5.86.

results.claim: Leave-one-out CV, GCV, Cp and k-fold CV all apply to local regression because it is a linear smoother with smoother matrix entries {S}_ij = l_i(x_j); effective df = trace(S)
results.setup: Sec 6.2; LOO CV derivation left as Exercise 6.7
results.quote:
Leave-
one-out cross-validation is particularly simple (Exercise 6.7), as is general-
ized cross-validation, Cp (Exercise 6.10), and k-fold cross-validation.

results.claim: Local regression is useful only up to about two or three dimensions: localness (low bias) and neighborhood size (low variance) cannot both be kept without exponentially growing sample size in p
results.quote:
Local regression becomes less useful in dimensions much higher than two
or three.

results.claim: Fraction of points near the boundary tends to one as dimension grows (curse of dimensionality), making boundary correction by local polynomials more important
results.quote:
one of the manifesta-
tions of the curse of dimensionality is that the fraction of points close to the
boundary increases to one as the dimension grows.

results.claim: Galaxy velocity example: local linear regression in R^2 with a nearest-neighbor window using 15% of the data on an irregular star-shaped design
results.quote:
using a
nearest-neighbor window with 15% of the data.

results.claim: Ozone trellis example: each conditioning panel holds about 40% of the range of each conditioned variable
results.setup: Fig 6.9, ozone vs radiation conditioned on temperature and wind
results.quote:
Each panel contains about 40% of the range of each of the condi-
tioned variables.

results.claim: Additive models can be fit by backfitting where each step is a one-dimensional local regression of the partial residual on X_k
results.quote:
The important detail is that at any
stage, one-dimensional local regression is all that is needed.

results.claim: Varying coefficient models f(X)=alpha(Z)+beta_1(Z)X1+...+beta_q(Z)Xq are fit by locally weighted least squares in Z (eq 6.17); aorta diameter vs age: thickening with age in upper aorta fades with distance down
results.setup: Fig 6.10/6.11, human aorta data, separate fits for males and females
results.quote:
While the aorta clearly
does thicken with age at the higher regions of the aorta, the relationship
fades with distance down the aorta.

results.claim: Any parametric model can be made local if the fitting method accepts observation weights (local likelihood, local multiclass logistic, local autoregression)
results.quote:
any
parametric model can be made local if the ﬁtting method ac-
commodates observation weights.

results.claim: Local linear logistic regression on South African heart disease data reveals an unexpected CHD prevalence rise at low blood pressure and obesity, explained as retrospective data with prior treatment
results.setup: Fig 6.12, univariate local logistic fits, CHD data of Chapter 4
results.quote:
The unexpected increase in the prevalence of CHD at
the lower ends of the ranges is because these are retrospective data

results.claim: Local logistic regression (tri-cube, k-NN bandwidth) beats Gaussian kernel density classification at high systolic BP where data are sparse, because the NN bandwidth widens the kernel
results.setup: Fig 6.14 vs Fig 6.12, CHD data, one predictor (SBP)
results.quote:
this effectively widens the kernel in this region, and makes use
of the local linear assumption to smooth out the estimate

results.claim: For classification, learning separate class densities well may be unnecessary or misleading; only the posterior near the decision boundary matters
results.setup: Sec 6.6.2, Fig 6.15 synthetic multimodal densities with smooth posterior
results.quote:
If classiﬁcation is the ultimate goal, then learning the separate class den-
sities well may be unnecessary, and can in fact be misleading.

results.claim: Naive Bayes often outperforms far more sophisticated alternatives despite its independence assumption, because bias in class densities need not hurt posteriors near the boundary
results.quote:
naive Bayes classiﬁers often
outperform far more sophisticated alternatives.

results.claim: Naive Bayes log-odds has generalized additive model form alpha_l + sum_k g_lk(X_k)
results.quote: This has the form of a generalized additive model

results.claim: Constant-width radial basis functions leave holes; renormalizing (eq 6.30) removes them; Nadaraya-Watson is an expansion in renormalized RBFs with xi_i=x_i, beta_i=y_i
results.quote:
creating holes—regions of IRp where none of the kernels has appreciable
support

results.claim: Two-component Gaussian mixture on Age (CHD data, fit by EM without labels): mu1=36.4, Sigma1=157.7, alpha1=0.7, mu2=58.0, Sigma2=15.6, alpha2=0.3
results.setup: Sec 6.8, Fig 6.17, heart disease data, scalar Sigma not constrained equal

results.claim: Thresholding the mixture component-2 responsibility at 0.5 gives the same 32% error vs CHD labels as linear logistic regression, though the mixture never saw labels
results.setup: Sec 6.8, Age as only feature, 2x2 table CHD x mixture class: No 232/70, Yes 76/84
results.quote:
achieves the same error rate (32%) when ﬁt to
these data using maximum-likelihood
results.note: Error computed from table (70+76)/462 = 31.6%, rounded by authors to 32%

results.claim: Cost of a kernel/local fit at one query point is O(N) flops; basis expansion costs O(M) per evaluation, M~O(log N), with initial cost at least O(NM^2+M^3); CV for lambda costs O(N^2)
results.quote: The computational cost to ﬁt at a single observation x0 is O(N) ﬂops

results.claim: loess and locfit compute the fit exactly at M carefully chosen locations (O(NM)) and interpolate by blending (O(M) per evaluation)
results.quote:
They compute the ﬁt exactly at M
carefully chosen locations (O(NM))

results.claim: Fig 6.1 simulation: 100 pairs from Y=sin(4X)+eps, X~U[0,1], eps~N(0,1/3); 30-NN running mean is discontinuous; Epanechnikov NW with lambda=0.2 is continuous
results.quote:
In
the left panel the green curve is the result of a 30-nearest-neighbor running-mean
smoother.

results.claim: Large lambda gives lower variance and higher bias; metric windows keep bias constant with variance inversely proportional to local density; nearest-neighbor windows keep variance constant
results.quote:
Large λ implies lower variance
(averages over more observations) but higher bias

limits: Chapter is expository; examples are illustrations with no benchmark comparisons or error tables except the 32% mixture error
Memory-based: model is the whole training set, fitting at prediction time, O(N) per query, can be infeasible for real-time use (Sec 6.9)
Local regression degrades beyond 2-3 dimensions without structural assumptions (Sec 6.3)
Boundary bias of local averages; local linear fits biased in curvature (Fig 6.5)
Metric-width Gaussian KDE is poor in sparse regions; Gaussian mixture likelihood unbounded (Ex 6.11)
Authors do not recommend mixing degrees (linear at boundary, quadratic inside) (p.198)
Software refs (S-PLUS loess, locfit) date the implementation advice
practices: Standardize each predictor to unit standard deviation before radial-kernel smoothing in R^p (Sec 6.3, p.200).
Prefer local linear to local constant (Nadaraya-Watson) for superior boundary performance (Sec 6.3, p.200).
Choose lambda by leave-one-out CV, GCV, Cp or k-fold CV; calibrate by trace(S_lambda) (Sec 6.2, p.199).
Do not mix local polynomial degrees across the domain; let the application choose, and use local linear for extrapolation (Sec 6.1.1, p.198).
Use renormalized RBFs when a constant width lambda is assumed, to avoid holes (Sec 6.7, p.213).
For classification, use local logistic regression or estimate posteriors near the boundary rather than separate class densities, which may mislead (Sec 6.6.2, p.210).
Use naive Bayes with 1-D kernel density estimates in high dimensions; histograms for discrete features (Sec 6.6.3, p.211).
Handle ties in x by averaging y and carrying a weight w_i that multiplies the kernel weight (Sec 6.1, p.193).
